questions.question: On grid paper, Ravi draws a rectangle that is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is the area of his rectangle?
questions.explain: Area of a rectangle = length × width, so 6 × 4 = 24 cm². The trap is 20 cm² — that is the perimeter (6+4+6+4), the distance around, not the space covered.

questions.question: A square tile has sides of 7 cm. What is the perimeter of the tile?
questions.explain: Perimeter means all the way around, so add all four sides: 7+7+7+7 = 28 cm. The trap is 49 cm — that is 7 × 7, which gives the area, not the perimeter.

questions.question: Mei covers a shape on a geoboard with square units. It is made of 5 rows with 3 squares in each row. What is the area of the shape?
questions.explain: Count the squares that cover the shape: 5 rows × 3 = 15 square units. The trap is 16 — that is the perimeter of this 5-by-3 rectangle, which counts the edge, not the squares inside.

questions.question: A rectangular whiteboard is 9 m long and 5 m wide. What is its perimeter?
questions.explain: Perimeter = 9 + 5 + 9 + 5 = 28 m, because every side gets counted. The trap is 45 m — that is 9 × 5, the area, and 14 m is only one length plus one width (half the way around).

questions.question: Students build a model of a Coast Salish longhouse. The rectangular floor is 12 m long and 6 m wide, and they want to cover the whole floor with cedar mats. How much floor do the mats need to cover?
questions.explain: Covering a floor means area: 12 × 6 = 72 m² (square metres, because it is a surface). The trap is 36 m² — 36 is the perimeter of the floor, which tells you the distance around the walls, not how much floor to cover.

questions.question: Nadia's family is putting a fence around a rectangular vegetable garden that is 7 m long and 4 m wide. Fencing costs $5 for each metre. How much will the fencing cost?
questions.explain: Fencing goes around the edge, so find the perimeter first: 7+4+7+4 = 22 m, then 22 × $5 = $110. The trap is $140 — that comes from using the area (7 × 4 = 28) instead of the perimeter.

questions.question: Owen has 24 square tiles that are each 1 m². He lays them all out with no gaps to make one rectangle that is 6 m long. What is the perimeter of the rectangle he makes?
questions.explain: The 24 tiles give an area of 24 m², so the width is 24 ÷ 6 = 4 m, and the perimeter is 6+4+6+4 = 20 m. The trap is 24 m — that is the area number reused, and area and perimeter are not the same measurement.

questions.question: A square sandbox at a Kelowna playground has a perimeter of 20 m. What is the area of the sandbox?
questions.explain: A square has 4 equal sides, so each side is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m, and the area is 5 × 5 = 25 m². The trap is 400 m² — that comes from multiplying the perimeter by itself instead of finding one side first.

questions.question: Two rectangular garden plots each use exactly 20 m of fencing. Plot A is 8 m long and 2 m wide. Plot B is 6 m long and 4 m wide. Which statement is true?
options: Plot A has the greater area, because it is longer.
The plots have the same area because they use the same amount of fencing.
Plot B has the greater area, by 8 m².
Plot B has the greater area, by 4 m².
questions.explain: Check both areas: Plot A is 8 × 2 = 16 m² and Plot B is 6 × 4 = 24 m², so B has 8 m² more. The big trap is thinking equal perimeters must mean equal areas — shapes with the same distance around can hold very different amounts of space.

questions.question: Jasmine is fencing a rectangular berry patch with an area of exactly 36 m². She wants to use the least amount of fencing. Which whole-number dimensions should she choose?
questions.explain: All four choices have an area of 36 m², so compare perimeters: 74 m, 40 m, 26 m, and 24 m — the 6 m by 6 m square uses the least fencing. The trap is assuming the same area means the same perimeter; the closer a rectangle is to a square, the shorter its perimeter.

questions.question: For a class display, Leo builds a rectangular model longhouse floor that measures 150 cm long and 80 cm wide. He wants to put ribbon all the way around the edge. How many metres of ribbon does he need?
questions.explain: Perimeter first: 150+80+150+80 = 460 cm, and since 100 cm = 1 m, that is 4.6 m of ribbon. The traps are forgetting the conversion or dividing by the wrong amount, and 1.2 is the area (1.5 m × 0.8 m), not the distance around.

questions.question: A rectangular deck behind a Nanaimo house measures 6 m by 4 m. A square hot tub with 2 m sides sits on one corner of the deck. How much of the deck is still open floor?
questions.explain: Find the deck's area, 6 × 4 = 24 m², then subtract the hot tub's area, 2 × 2 = 4 m², leaving 20 m². The trap is 16 m² — that comes from subtracting the hot tub's perimeter (8 m) instead of its area.
